summary.text: A 60-year-old woman was admitted to the Department of Internal Diseases with mild pain at the lower abdomen and the right iliac fossa. Blood tests, including WBC 8.01 K/μL with 76.3% neutrophils, were within normal limits, and abdominal X-ray and ultrasound did not reveal any abnormalities. She had no fever or anorexia, McBurney sign was negative, and the same clinical condition had occurred several times in the past and was treated conservatively with success.

Examination by a surgeon was also realized because the initial condition could resemble mild appendicitis. General practitioners considered a possible bowel inflammation and considered initial rehydration and empirical antibiotic administration necessary. Based on the repeated clinical history, colonoscopy was programmed within the same admission; the procedure was uneventful and examination up to 10 cm proximally to the ileocecal valve led to no pathologic findings.

Mild abdominal pain reoccurred 10 hours after the colonoscopy and presented as acute abdomen 24 hours after the procedure, especially to the right side, with flatulence but still without fever or white blood cell count disturbance (WBC 9.02 K/μL). A new abdominal X-ray showed free abdominal gas, and CT showed diffuse inflammation in the area of the appendix and the retroperitoneal space, free gas in the peritoneal cavity and a perihepatic collection.

An exploratory laparotomy revealed perforated appendicitis with peritonitis; an appendectomy was performed and the cavity was rinsed and drained. The authors considered the condition a postcolonoscopy complication. The patient remained hemodynamically stable with normal temperature and blood laboratory results and was discharged on the tenth postoperative day in good health condition.

ambiguities.issue: The authors support a fecalith, possibly introduced by air insufflation, as the causal event, but state that a fecalith already present before the colonoscopy and perforation due to overinsufflation or scope trauma could not be excluded; they also call the intraoperative condition a postcolonoscopy complication and say peritonitis could be explained by the 20-hour interval from mild postcolonoscopy symptoms to surgical management.

evidence.quote: We support that the causal event was the fecalith that could be introduced into the appendix by the air insufflation.
the possibility of the presence of the fecalith in the appendix prior to the colonoscopy could not be excluded
we can also not exclude the fact that perforation could be due to overinsufflation or trauma from the scope
Due to the interference of the colonoscopy, with no abnormal findings until and during its realization, we considered the intraoperative condition as a postcolonoscopy complication.

ambiguities.must_not_infer: Do not record a fecalith, overinsufflation, scope trauma, delayed surgery or the colonoscopy as the established cause of the perforation or peritonitis.

ambiguities.issue: The severe symptoms and the mild postcolonoscopy symptoms used for the six-hour and 20-hour intervals are not explicitly identified with the acute abdomen presentation or the recurrent abdominal pain.

evidence.quote: The time interval between the presence of severe symptoms and surgery included the realization of X-ray and CT imaging and was about six hours.
the interval of 20 hours from the moment of the presence of mild postcolonoscopy symptoms until the surgical management

ambiguities.must_not_infer: Do not merge the interval statements into the acute abdomen or recurrent pain facts or derive times from them.

ambiguities.issue: The Figure 5 caption lists a fecalith and the Discussion lists impacted stool in the appendix found after the open appendectomy; the text does not state they are the same finding. The caption also names the intraoperative finding acute appendicitis with peritonitis while the case text says perforated appendicitis with peritonitis.

evidence.quote: Intraoperative findings. Acute appendicitis with peritonitis. Presence of a fecalith.
followed by the finding of impacted stool in the appendix after the open appendectomy
during which perforated appendicitis with peritonitis was revealed

ambiguities.must_not_infer: Do not equate the fecalith with the impacted stool, and do not read the caption as saying the appendix was not perforated.

ambiguities.issue: The WBC and neutrophil values in the acute abdomen sentence have no stated sampling time, and only the white blood cell count is classified (without white blood cell count disturbance).

evidence.quote: still without fever or white blood cell count disturbance (WBC: 9.02 K/μL, neutrophils: 78.6%)

ambiguities.must_not_infer: Do not assign a time to these values or a flag to the neutrophil percentage.

ambiguities.issue: Colonoscopy findings from the appendix are called normal in the Discussion while the case text gives the examined extent as up to 10 cm proximally to the ileocecal valve.

evidence.quote: In our case, colonoscopy findings from the appendix were normal
examination up to 10 cm proximally to the ileocecal valve did not lead to any pathologic findings

ambiguities.must_not_infer: Do not infer whether the appendiceal orifice was visualized.

article_limitations: Table 1 holds 38 rows (37 published literature cases plus the authors' own case) without labelling the index row; no Table 1 cell is recorded as an index-patient fact (see the patient ambiguity).
Discussion cohort statistics (38 patients, sex and age summaries, treatment and condition counts) are aggregate literature-review content and are not copied to the individual.
Source conflict: the Discussion states no symptoms prior to the procedure while the abstract and case text describe abdominal pain before the colonoscopy; both sides are review_only.
Whether the general practitioners' rehydration and empirical antibiotic administration were actually given is not stated beyond considered necessary; action recorded as unknown.
The WBC and neutrophil values in the acute abdomen sentence have no stated sampling time; the neutrophil percentage carries no source classification.

Authors' etiologic statements (fecalith, overinsufflation, scope trauma, 20-hour interval, postcolonoscopy complication) are hedged hypotheses and are recorded as possible or review_only, not as established causes.
Annotation figures keep caption-level status not_inspected; the five JPEGs were inspected in the separate visual target.
The article lists no supplementary material.
